name: Tatar khanates (Kazan, Astrakhan, Sibir, Nogai)
summary: Successor states of the Golden Horde on the Volga and in western Siberia; Ivan the Terrible conquered Kazan (1552) and Astrakhan (1556), Cossacks took Sibir (1582–98), and the Nogai Horde broke up in the 1600s.

location.value: Kazan Khanate: contemporary Tatarstan, Mari El, Chuvashia, Mordovia and parts of Udmurtia and Bashkortostan.

terrain.value: Forest-steppe along the middle Volga (Kazan), the lower Volga delta (Astrakhan), western Siberian forests (Sibir) and open steppe (Nogai).

climate.value: Continental: cold winters and hot summers.

resources.value: Furs, fish (sturgeon), horses, salt and grain.

disasters.value: Harsh winters, famine and plague hit the region.

urbanisation.value: Kazan and Astrakhan were trading towns; Sibir’s capital Isker was small.

migration.value: Nogai nomads moved across the steppe; many Tatars resettled after the Russian conquest.

economicBase.value: In the 16th century Russia was Kazan’s main trading partner, with markets such as the Taşayaq Bazaar and a fair on the Volga; prisoners of war were usually sold abroad.

tradeRoutes.value: The Volga route linking Russia, Persia and Central Asia.

wealth.value: Trade wealth came from the Volga trade at Kazan and Astrakhan.

moneyAndTax.value: Silver coins; tribute (yasak) in furs from forest peoples.

inequality.value: Rulers and military elites above farmers and herders.

governmentType.value: The khan governed with a cabinet council (Diwan); nobles held ranks such as beg, emir and morza.

keyRulers.value: Ulugh Muhammad founded the Khanate of Kazan, taking the throne around 1437–1438.

succession.value: Chinggisid princes chosen with the backing of noble clans, often under Moscow or Crimea’s influence.

stability.value: Unstable: pro-Moscow and pro-Crimea factions fought over the thrones.

armyAndTech.value: Horse archers, with some firearms in the 1500s.

majorWars.value: Ivan III occupied Kazan in July 1487 and seated a puppet; Kazan made a mutual-aid treaty with Astrakhan in 1521; the Russians entered Kazan on 3 October 1552 and dismantled its administration.

alliancesRivals.value: Crimean Khanate and the Ottomans against Muscovy.

scienceEducation.value: Madrasas taught Islamic law and Turkic literature.

openness.value: Open to trade with Russia and Persia.

communicationTransport.value: River boats on the Volga; horses on the steppe.

languageWriting.value: Tatar and other Kipchak Turkic languages, written in Arabic script.

artsArchitecture.value: Mosques and the Kazan kremlin (rebuilt after 1552).

socialStructure.value: Khans, beys, townspeople, farmers and nomads.

sharedIdentity.value: A Muslim Tatar identity, set against Orthodox Russia.

dailyLife.value: Horse meat, mare’s milk (kumis) and bread.

neighbours.value: Muscovy, Crimea, the Kazakh Khanate and Siberian peoples.

ideasReligions.value: Islam spread among the Volga peoples.

riseSignals.value: Ulugh Muhammad took the Kazan throne in 1437 or 1438 (infobox 1438), finalised by his son in 1445; a successor state of the Golden Horde with its capital at Kazan.

peakPeriod.value: The Crimean Khanate page names no peak; its map shows the limit of expansion in 1523. Devlet I Giray burned Moscow in 1571. The claim about Kazan dominating Moscow is unchecked.

declineSignals.value: The Russian conquest of Kazan in 1552.

outcome.value: Ivan IV conquered Kazan in 1552; Russian troops entered the city on 3 October 1552.

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles; population figures are estimates.
